standard.title: Compound sentences
standard.description: understand that connections can be made between ideas by using a compound sentence with 2 or more independent clauses usually linked by a coordinating conjunction
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand that a simple sentence is a single independent clause representing one event or idea (AC9E1LA06). They have not yet connected independent clauses into compound sentences or understood how coordinating conjunctions signal the relationship between clauses.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can understand that compound sentences connect two or more independent clauses using coordinating conjunctions, and can identify the relationship between ideas that each conjunction signals.

nodes.label: Independent clauses can be joined
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that a compound sentence contains two or more complete ideas, each of which could stand alone, joined by a linking word.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the two independent clauses in a given compound sentence and confirm that each makes sense on its own.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and construct compound sentences from pairs of simple sentences across a range of topics; verify that each clause is independent.
wider: Sort a set of sentences into simple and compound, explaining the reasoning
Identify compound sentences in familiar picture books and shared reading texts
success_criteria: Student can identify both independent clauses in a compound sentence.
Student can confirm that each clause makes sense without the other.

nodes.label: Conjunctions signal relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how 'and', 'but' and 'so' each signal a different relationship between ideas — addition, contrast and consequence — and choose the correct conjunction for a given pair of clauses.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify whether 'and', 'but' or 'so' is appropriate to connect two given clauses and explain the relationship.
nodes.typical_width: Construct compound sentences using 'and', 'but' and 'so', explaining the relationship each conjunction signals; identify these conjunctions in a range of texts.
wider: Compare sentences where the conjunction is changed (e.g. 'and' to 'but') and discuss how meaning changes
Identify compound sentences in informative texts and discuss whether the conjunction was the best choice

response_modes.reason: Students often default to 'and' for any conjunction slot, treating compound sentences as mere addition. Exposure to multiple contexts where 'but' (contrast) or 'so' (consequence) is required — and where the wrong conjunction changes meaning — resolves the over-reliance on 'and'. More contrasting examples, not more practice with 'and', is the productive move.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The relationship-signalling function of conjunctions is a genuinely rich direction — it connects to argument, cause-and-effect and narrative turn, all of which students encounter across curriculum areas. Exploring how the same pair of clauses reads differently with different conjunctions is meaningful widening.
success_criteria: Student selects the correct conjunction for a given relationship between two clauses.
Student can name the relationship ('and' = addition, 'but' = contrast, 'so' = consequence) for at least two conjunctions.

nodes.label: Constructing compound sentences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct their own compound sentences, connecting independent clauses with appropriate coordinating conjunctions to express related ideas clearly.
nodes.minimum_width: Write at least two compound sentences using different conjunctions ('and', 'but', 'so') in a short piece of writing.
nodes.typical_width: Use compound sentences with varied conjunctions flexibly across simple and compound sentence writing, adjusting conjunction choice to signal intended relationships.
wider: Experiment with compound sentences of three clauses (e.g. 'The wolf huffed / and he puffed / and he blew the house down!') and discuss the rhythmic effect
Revise a piece of writing by converting some simple sentences to compound sentences where the relationship between ideas warrants it

response_modes.reason: Constructing compound sentences correctly — ensuring both clauses are independent, choosing the right conjunction — requires practice and checking. Errors at this node (run-on sentences, clause-merging errors, wrong conjunction) propagate into written text production. Precision-focused practice is the productive investment here.

nodes.hinge_reason: Compound sentence errors — run-on sentences, dependent clause errors, wrong conjunction — propagate into all written text production. Students who cannot construct these reliably carry grammatical incoherence into every subsequent writing task.
success_criteria: Student produces a compound sentence where both clauses are independent and the conjunction is appropriate.
Student does not produce a run-on sentence or a sentence where one clause is dependent.
